kafka-architecture.tldr:
• Kafka is a partitioned, replicated commit log; consumers pull by offset and data stays until retention.
  • Partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordering; consumer groups split partitions among members.
  • Leaders serve reads and writes; ISR followers replicate; KRaft replaced ZooKeeper.
  • Speed comes from sequential I/O, the page cache, zero-copy and batching.
kafka-architecture.body:
Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Producers append records; consumers read at their own pace by offset; records stay for a configured retention, regardless of whether anyone consumed them.

Concept Meaning
Broker a Kafka server; a cluster has many
Topic named stream of records (category)
Partition ordered, append-only log; the unit of parallelism and ordering
Offset position of a record within a partition (monotonic)
Record key, value, headers, timestamp
Replication factor copies of each partition across brokers (typically 3)
Leader / followers leader serves reads and writes; followers replicate
ISR in-sync replicas: followers caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms
Consumer group set of consumers sharing the work; each partition goes to exactly one member
Controller broker managing partition leadership and metadata
KRaft Raft-based metadata quorum replacing ZooKeeper (ZooKeeper removed in Kafka 4.0)

Why Kafka is fast: sequential disk appends; the OS page cache instead of a JVM cache; zero-copy (sendfile) from page cache to socket; batching and compression of record batches end to end; partitions spread load across brokers; consumers pull (no per-message broker bookkeeping, just an offset per group-partition).

Storage: each partition is a directory of segments (.log data, .index offset index, .timeindex). Only the active segment is written; retention deletes or compacts whole old segments.

A segment file is named after its base offset, so finding offset 50,000 is a binary search over file names, then a lookup in the sparse .index (every ~4 KB) and a short scan. Segments roll at segment.bytes (1 GB) or segment.ms. Because retention works on whole segments, a record can outlive retention.ms until its segment closes.

Topic → partitions → replicas across brokers

Leadership is spread so each broker leads some partitions and follows others: load is balanced and losing one broker only moves the leadership of the partitions it led. With broker.rack set, replicas land on different racks / availability zones.

kafka-replication.tldr:
• Each partition has one leader; followers fetch from it, and the ISR is the set that has caught up.
  • Consumers read only up to the high watermark, so they never see records a failover could lose.
  • acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 on RF=3 survives one broker failure without losing acknowledged writes.
  • Leader epochs let a returning ex-leader truncate divergent records; keep unclean leader election off for critical data.
kafka-replication.body:
Every partition has one leader and replication.factor − 1 followers. Producers and (by default) consumers talk only to the leader; followers continuously fetch from it, exactly like consumers.

In-sync replicas (ISR) are the leader plus every follower that has caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s). Only ISR members are eligible to become leader without data loss.

  • Log end offset (LEO) — next offset to be written on that replica.
  • High watermark (HW) — the smallest LEO across the ISR. Records below it are committed: consumers can read only up to the HW, so they never see data that could disappear in a failover.
  • A record acknowledged with acks=all is below the HW on every ISR member.

ISR shrink and min.insync.replicas

Leader failover

The leader epoch stamps every batch with the leadership generation, so a returning ex-leader knows exactly where its log diverged and truncates uncommitted records instead of creating split-brain divergence.

Unclean leader election. If no ISR member is alive, Kafka can either wait (default, unclean.leader.election.enable=false: partition offline, no data loss) or elect an out-of-sync replica (available, but acknowledged records are lost). Choose consistency for payments, availability perhaps for metrics.

KRaft. Since Kafka 3.3 (and exclusively in 4.0) cluster metadata — topics, partitions, ISR, configs — lives in an internal Raft-replicated log (__cluster_metadata) on a small quorum of controller nodes, instead of ZooKeeper. Brokers follow that log, so failover and startup are much faster and clusters can hold millions of partitions.

Follower fetching (KIP-392). With replica.selector.class=RackAwareReplicaSelector and client.rack on consumers, consumers can read from a follower in their own availability zone — cutting cross-AZ network cost — at the price of slightly higher latency up to the HW.

Interview tip "Can Kafka lose acknowledged data?" Not with acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, RF=3 and unclean election disabled — unless two brokers holding the data lose their disks at once. Because Kafka acks once data is in the page cache of each ISR member (not fsynced), it relies on replication rather than fsync for durability; a simultaneous power loss of all replicas is the remaining risk.

kafka-ordering.tldr:
• Order is guaranteed only within a partition; use the entity id as the key.
  • Changing the partition count remaps keys and breaks per-key ordering across the change.
  • Hot keys overload one partition.
  • Idempotence keeps retries from reordering records.
kafka-ordering.body:
Kafka guarantees order only within a partition. The default partitioner sends records with the same key to the same partition (murmur2(key) % numPartitions), so all events for one entity stay ordered.

Java
// All events for order 42 land in the same partition -> processed in order
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", order.getId().toString(), event);
  • No key: Kafka 2.4+ uses the sticky partitioner (fill a batch for one partition, then switch), spreading load without per-record round robin.
  • Changing the partition count changes hash % N, so keys move to different partitions and per-key ordering breaks across the change. Over-provision partitions up front.
  • Hot keys overload one partition; spread with a composite key if strict ordering per key isn't needed.

Choosing the key — common patterns

Need Key Why
order lifecycle events in order orderId all events of one order in one partition
per-customer ordering (balance updates) customerId ordering across a customer's orders
maximum spread, no ordering need null sticky partitioner balances batches
multi-tenant fairness tenantId + ":" + entityId avoids one big tenant pinning a partition while keeping entity order

How many partitions? Enough for target throughput and consumer parallelism: partitions ≥ max(target MB/s ÷ per-partition producer MB/s, target MB/s ÷ per-consumer MB/s), and at least the max number of consumers you'll run in a group. Too many partitions cost broker memory, file handles, and longer leader elections.

Pitfall with max.in.flight.requests.per.connection > 1 and retries but no idempotence, a failed batch can be retried after a later batch succeeded, reordering records. Enable idempotence (default since Kafka 3.0).

kafka-producer.tldr:
• send() batches per partition; a Sender thread ships batches to leaders.
  • Durable settings: acks=all, idempotence on, min.insync.replicas=2 with RF 3, no unclean leader election.
  • Throughput: linger.ms, batch.size, compression.type=zstd/lz4.
  • Keep send callbacks fast; they run on the I/O thread.
kafka-producer.body:
send() is asynchronous: records are serialized, partitioned and appended to an in-memory batch; a background Sender thread ships batches to partition leaders.

What acks means on the wire

Idempotent retry — why there's no duplicate

Key settings

Config Meaning Production value
acks 0 no ack; 1 leader wrote it; all all ISR wrote it all
enable.idempotence broker dedups retries using producer id + sequence numbers true (default 3.0+)
retries retry transient errors default (Integer.MAX_VALUE), bounded by delivery.timeout.ms
delivery.timeout.ms total time to deliver, including retries 120000
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection unacked batches per connection ≤ 5 with idempotence keeps order
batch.size max bytes per partition batch 32–64 KB for throughput
linger.ms wait to fill a batch 5–20 ms
compression.type none, gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd lz4 or zstd
buffer.memory / max.block.ms memory for unsent records; how long send blocks when full tune for bursts

Durability needs broker-side settings too: min.insync.replicas=2 with replication factor 3 and acks=all means a write succeeds only if at least 2 replicas have it; with fewer ISR the producer gets NotEnoughReplicasException instead of silently losing data. Keep unclean.leader.election.enable=false so an out-of-sync replica can't become leader and drop committed records.

Durability matrix

acks min.insync.replicas (RF=3) Survives Availability cost
0 any nothing guaranteed none
1 any broker restart if followers caught up; loses data if leader dies first none
all 1 same as acks=1 when ISR has shrunk to the leader none
all 2 any single broker failure, no acknowledged loss writes fail if 2 brokers down
all 3 two failures… but any single broker down blocks writes high
Java
Properties p = new Properties();
p.put(ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092");
p.put(ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class);
p.put(ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class);
p.put(ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all");
p.put(ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, true);
p.put(ProducerConfig.LINGER_MS_CONFIG, 10);
p.put(ProducerConfig.COMPRESSION_TYPE_CONFIG, "zstd");

try (KafkaProducer<String, String> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(p)) {
    producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", "42", payload), (meta, ex) -> {
        if (ex != null) log.error("send failed", ex);       // callback runs on the I/O thread: keep it fast
        else log.debug("p{} @{}", meta.partition(), meta.offset());
    });
}

kafka-consumer.tldr:
• Commit after processing for at-least-once; make processing idempotent.
  • max.poll.interval.ms exceeded → the consumer leaves the group → rebalance and duplicates.
  • Use cooperative sticky assignment and static membership to reduce rebalances.
  • More consumers than partitions sit idle.
kafka-consumer.body:
Consumers pull with poll(). Within a group, each partition is assigned to one consumer; extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle. Different groups each receive every record (pub-sub).

Offsets are committed per group-partition to the internal __consumer_offsets topic. The committed offset is the next record to read.

If this consumer crashes now, its replacement restarts at offset 3, so records 3–5 are processed again: that's at-least-once, and why consumers must be idempotent.

Partition assignment within a group

Java
Properties c = new Properties();
c.put(ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "kafka-1:9092");
c.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "billing");
c.put(ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG, false);            // commit after processing
c.put(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest");         // when no committed offset
c.put(ConsumerConfig.MAX_POLL_RECORDS_CONFIG, 200);
c.put(ConsumerConfig.PARTITION_ASSIGNMENT_STRATEGY_CONFIG, CooperativeStickyAssignor.class.getName());
c.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class);
c.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class);

try (KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(c)) {
    consumer.subscribe(List.of("orders"));
    while (running) {
        ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
        for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) process(r);   // idempotent!
        consumer.commitSync();                                          // at-least-once
    }
}

Commit timing decides semantics

  • Commit after processing → at-least-once (a crash before commit replays records). The standard choice, paired with idempotent processing.
  • Commit before processing → at-most-once (a crash after commit loses records).
  • Auto-commit commits periodically during poll(), so it can be either; avoid for important data.

Liveness settings

Config Meaning
session.timeout.ms (45 s default) no heartbeat within this → consumer considered dead
heartbeat.interval.ms heartbeats are sent by a background thread
max.poll.interval.ms (5 min default) max time between poll() calls; exceeding it → consumer leaves the group
max.poll.records records per poll; lower it if processing is slow

Rebalancing reassigns partitions when consumers join, leave, crash or exceed max.poll.interval.ms, or when partitions are added.

Use a ConsumerRebalanceListener (or Spring's ConsumerAwareRebalanceListener) to commit processed offsets in onPartitionsRevoked, otherwise the new owner reprocesses everything since the last commit.

  • Eager rebalancing (old default): everyone revokes everything, a stop-the-world pause.
  • Cooperative sticky (incremental): only moved partitions are revoked; others keep consuming.
  • Static membership (group.instance.id): a restarting pod rejoins with the same identity within the session timeout without triggering a rebalance (great for rolling deploys).
  • Kafka 4.0's new consumer group protocol (KIP-848, group.protocol=consumer) moves assignment to the broker and makes rebalances incremental by default.

Pitfall slow processing (a long DB call per record × 500 records) exceeds max.poll.interval.ms; the consumer gets kicked, its partitions rebalance, uncommitted records are reprocessed by someone else, and the cycle repeats: a rebalance storm with duplicates. Lower max.poll.records, speed up processing, or hand work to a bounded pool while pausing the partition.

kafka-semantics.tldr:
• Idempotent producers dedup retries per partition using producer ids and sequence numbers.
  • Transactions commit output records and consumer offsets atomically; readers use read_committed.
  • Kafka EOS covers Kafka-to-Kafka only; external side effects still need idempotency or the outbox.
  • A stable transactional.id fences zombie producers.

kafka-spring.tldr:
• Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer so poison pills don't loop forever.
  • DefaultErrorHandler with exponential backoff and DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer sends failures to a DLT.
  • @RetryableTopic gives non-blocking retries at the cost of per-key ordering.
  • Batch listeners enable bulk DB writes.
kafka-spring.body:
YAML
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 10
        compression.type: zstd
    consumer:
      group-id: billing
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.shop.events"
        partition.assignment.strategy: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
    listener:
      ack-mode: record          # commit after each record is processed successfully
      concurrency: 3            # 3 consumer threads (<= partitions)

ErrorHandlingDeserializer wraps the real deserializer so a malformed message (poison pill) becomes a handled error instead of crashing the listener in an endless loop.

Producer

Java
@Service
public class OrderEventPublisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> template;
    public OrderEventPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> template) { this.template = template; }

    public CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, OrderEvent>> publish(OrderEvent e) {
        ProducerRecord<String, OrderEvent> rec = new ProducerRecord<>("orders", e.orderId(), e);
        rec.headers().add("eventId", e.eventId().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return template.send(rec).whenComplete((res, ex) -> {
            if (ex != null) log.error("publish failed for {}", e.orderId(), ex);
        });
    }
}

Listener with blocking retries + Dead Letter Topic

Java
@Configuration
public class KafkaErrorConfig {
    @Bean
    public DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
            (rec, ex) -> new TopicPartition(rec.topic() + ".DLT", rec.partition()));
        var backoff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3);
        backoff.setInitialInterval(1_000);
        backoff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backoff);
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class,   // don't retry bad data
                                          DeserializationException.class);
        return handler;                       // Boot wires a single DefaultErrorHandler bean automatically
    }
}

@Component
public class BillingListener {
    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing")
    public void onOrder(@Payload OrderEvent event,
                        @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_PARTITION) int partition,
                        @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset) {
        billing.invoice(event);               // throw -> retried 3x, then sent to orders.DLT
    }
}

Non-blocking retries (retry topics) — failed records go to orders-retry-1000, orders-retry-2000… so the main partition keeps flowing. Trade-off: per-key ordering is lost for retried records.

Blocking vs non-blocking retries

Blocking (DefaultErrorHandler + backoff) Non-blocking (@RetryableTopic)
Partition while retrying paused on that record keeps flowing
Per-key ordering preserved lost for retried records
Long backoff (minutes) risks max.poll.interval.ms fine
Extra topics only DLT one per retry level + DLT
Use for ordering-sensitive, short transient errors independent events, slow downstream recovery
Java
@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4",
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0),
    exclude = ValidationException.class,
    dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR)
@KafkaListener(topics = "payments", groupId = "ledger")
public void onPayment(PaymentEvent e) { ledger.post(e); }

@DltHandler
public void onDlt(PaymentEvent e, @Header(KafkaHeaders.EXCEPTION_MESSAGE) String reason) {
    alerting.raise("payment " + e.id() + " dead-lettered: " + reason);
}

Batch listener: @KafkaListener(batch = "true") void onBatch(List<OrderEvent> events) for bulk DB writes. A BatchListenerFailedException(index) tells the error handler which record failed.

kafka-retention.tldr:
• Delete policy removes old segments by time or size; slow consumers past retention lose data.
  • Compaction keeps the latest value per key; null values are tombstones.
  • Use Avro/Protobuf with a Schema Registry and compatibility rules.
  • Events carry an id, type, timestamp, schema version and aggregate key.
kafka-retention.body:
Retention (cleanup.policy=delete): delete segments older than retention.ms (default 7 days) or beyond retention.bytes. Consumers that fall further behind than retention lose data (auto.offset.reset kicks in).

Log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact): keep at least the latest value per key; older values for the same key are removed in the background. A record with a null value is a tombstone that deletes the key (after delete.retention.ms). Perfect for changelogs and current-state topics: user profiles, configuration, Kafka Streams state stores, __consumer_offsets itself.

Offsets are preserved (gaps appear); only the latest value per key survives, so a new consumer reading from the beginning rebuilds current state without replaying all history.

Shell
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic customer-profiles --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config cleanup.policy=compact --config min.insync.replicas=2 \
  --bootstrap-server kafka:9092

Schemas and evolution: use Avro or Protobuf with a Schema Registry. Producers register schemas; records carry a schema id; consumers deserialize with the right version. Compatibility modes: BACKWARD (new consumers read old data — add optional fields with defaults, remove fields), FORWARD (old consumers read new data), FULL (both). Plain JSON has no enforced contract and breaks consumers silently.

Event design tips: include eventId, eventType, occurredAt, schemaVersion, and the aggregate id as key; decide between thin events (id only, consumers call back) and fat events (full state, consumers stay decoupled).

kafka-ecosystem.tldr:
• Kafka Connect moves data in and out of Kafka with configured source and sink connectors, no custom code.
  • Debezium CDC streams row changes from the database log and is the most robust outbox relay.
  • Kafka Streams is a library for stateful processing inside your service, backed by RocksDB and changelog topics.
  • A table is the latest value per key of a stream; KStream–KTable joins enrich events without remote calls.
kafka-ecosystem.body:
Kafka Connect — a framework for moving data in and out of Kafka without writing producers and consumers: source connectors (database, files, SaaS → Kafka) and sink connectors (Kafka → Elasticsearch, S3, warehouse). Workers run in a distributed cluster, store their configs/offsets/status in Kafka topics, and rebalance tasks on failure.

Change Data Capture (CDC) with Debezium reads the database's replication log (Postgres WAL via logical decoding, MySQL binlog) and emits one event per row change with before, after, op (c/u/d) and source metadata. Nothing is polled and no application code changes. CDC is the most robust way to implement the transactional outbox: the service writes the business row and an outbox row in one DB transaction; Debezium's outbox event router publishes the outbox rows to Kafka.

JSON
{
  "before": { "id": 42, "status": "PLACED" },
  "after":  { "id": 42, "status": "PAID" },
  "op": "u",
  "source": { "table": "orders", "lsn": 23983421, "txId": 9812 },
  "ts_ms": 1760000000000
}

Kafka Streams — a Java library (not a cluster) for stateful stream processing inside your service: filter, map, join, aggregate and window, with local state stores (RocksDB) backed by compacted changelog topics, and exactly-once with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2.

Java
StreamsBuilder b = new StreamsBuilder();
KStream<String, Payment> payments = b.stream("payments");

payments.filter((k, p) -> p.status() == Status.CAPTURED)
        .groupBy((k, p) -> p.merchantId())
        .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
        .aggregate(() -> BigDecimal.ZERO,
                   (merchant, p, total) -> total.add(p.amount()),
                   Materialized.with(Serdes.String(), bigDecimalSerde))
        .toStream()
        .map((w, total) -> KeyValue.pair(w.key(), new MerchantVolume(w.key(), w.window().start(), total)))
        .to("merchant-volume-per-minute");
Tool Runs as Good for
Kafka Connect separate worker cluster, config only integration: DB → Kafka → sinks
Kafka Streams library inside your Java service per-service stateful processing, joins, windows
Apache Flink separate cluster large-scale stream processing, event-time, complex windows, SQL
ksqlDB server, SQL over streams quick SQL transformations

Stream–table duality: a stream is the changelog of a table; a table is the latest value per key of a stream (KTable, compacted topics). Joining a KStream of orders with a KTable of customers enriches events with current customer data without calling another service.

kafka-operations.tldr:
• Consumer lag is the key metric; alert on its growth.
  • Fix lag by scaling consumers (up to partitions), speeding processing, or adding partitions.
  • Watch under-replicated partitions, offline partitions and ISR shrinks on brokers.
  • Kafka is a replayable log; RabbitMQ is a routing broker that deletes on ack.
kafka-operations.body:
Consumer lag = log-end offset − committed offset per partition. The single most important consumer metric. Growing lag means consumers can't keep up.

Diagnosing lag — decision flow

Shell
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group billing
# GROUP   TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
# billing orders  0          10452           10460           8     consumer-1-...

# Replay: reset offsets (group must be inactive)
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-20T00:00:00.000 --execute

Fixing lag: add consumers (up to the partition count) → add partitions (breaks key mapping) → make processing faster (batch DB writes, async I/O, remove N+1) → parallelize within a partition while preserving key order (Confluent Parallel Consumer).

Throughput tuning

  • Producer: linger.ms 5–50, batch.size 64–256 KB, compression.type=zstd/lz4.
  • Consumer: fetch.min.bytes and fetch.max.wait.ms to fetch bigger chunks; max.poll.records sized to processing time.
  • Broker: enough partitions, fast disks, num.network.threads/num.io.threads, rack awareness.

Latency tuning: linger.ms=0, smaller batches, acks=1 only if you accept possible loss.

Broker health metrics: under-replicated partitions (should be 0), offline partitions, active controller count (exactly 1), ISR shrink/expand rate, request latency, disk usage.

Common production issues

Symptom Likely cause
Duplicates after deploys rebalance + at-least-once; consumers not idempotent
Lag spikes every few minutes processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms → rebalances
NotEnoughReplicasException ISR below min.insync.replicas (broker down or slow)
RecordTooLargeException message above max.request.size / message.max.bytes — store payload in S3, send a reference
One consumer busy, others idle hot key or fewer partitions than consumers
Listener stuck on one record poison pill without ErrorHandlingDeserializer/DLT

Kafka vs RabbitMQ

Kafka RabbitMQ
Model distributed log; consumers pull and track offsets broker pushes; messages deleted after ack
Replay yes, within retention no (streams feature aside)
Ordering per partition per queue (single consumer)
Routing by topic/partition rich (exchanges: direct, topic, fanout, headers)
Throughput very high (millions/s) high (tens of thousands/s per queue)
Best for event streaming, event sourcing, CDC, analytics pipelines task queues, RPC, complex routing, per-message TTL/priority

qa.q: How does Kafka guarantee message ordering?
qa.a: Only within a partition: records are appended and read sequentially by offset. To order related events, give them the same key so they land in the same partition, and keep idempotence enabled so retries don't reorder. There's no ordering across partitions.

qa.q: What happens when a consumer in a group dies?
qa.a: It stops heartbeating; after session.timeout.ms the group coordinator removes it and triggers a rebalance. Its partitions are reassigned to remaining members, which resume from the last committed offsets, so uncommitted processed records are reprocessed (at-least-once).

qa.q: How do you achieve exactly-once semantics in Kafka?
qa.a: Idempotent producer (dedups retries per partition) plus transactions that atomically write output records and the consumer offsets (sendOffsetsToTransaction), with downstream consumers using read_committed. For external side effects (DB, APIs) use idempotent consumers or outbox/inbox, since Kafka transactions can't include them.

qa.q: What is ISR and how do acks=all and min.insync.replicas work together?
qa.a: ISR is the set of replicas caught up with the leader. With acks=all, the leader acknowledges only after all current ISR members have the record. min.insync.replicas=2 (RF=3) rejects writes if fewer than 2 replicas are in sync, so an acknowledged write always exists on at least two brokers.

qa.q: What is consumer lag and how do you reduce it?
qa.a: The difference between the latest offset and the group's committed offset. Reduce it by scaling consumers up to the partition count, increasing partitions, optimizing processing (batching, async I/O, fewer DB round trips), and tuning fetch/poll sizes. Alert on lag growth, not absolute values.

qa.q: Can you have more consumers than partitions?
qa.a: Yes, but each partition is consumed by at most one member of a group, so the extra consumers stay idle (useful only as hot standbys). Parallelism is capped by partition count.

qa.q: How do you handle poison pill messages?
qa.a: Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer so deserialization failures become handled errors, configure a DefaultErrorHandler with bounded retries and a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, mark validation errors as non-retryable, and monitor/alert on the DLT with a replay tool.

A cleanup policy that keeps at least the latest record for each key and removes older ones, with null-value tombstones deleting keys. It turns a topic into a durable changelog of current state (profiles, configs, state stores) that a new consumer can read to rebuild the latest snapshot.

qa.q: Explain rebalancing and how to minimize its impact.
qa.a: Partition reassignment within a group when membership or subscriptions change. Minimize with the cooperative sticky assignor (incremental), static membership (group.instance.id) for restarts, keeping processing well under max.poll.interval.ms, graceful shutdown that commits and leaves the group, and the new broker-side consumer protocol in Kafka 4.x.

qa.q: Kafka vs RabbitMQ — when to use which?
qa.a: Kafka for high-throughput event streams, replayable history, event sourcing, CDC and multiple independent consumers of the same data. RabbitMQ for work queues, complex routing, per-message acknowledgement/priority/TTL and request-reply. Kafka keeps data after consumption; RabbitMQ deletes it on ack.

qa.q: How do you choose the number of partitions?
qa.a: From throughput targets and consumer parallelism: target throughput ÷ per-partition throughput (measured for both producers and consumers), at least the max consumer count, with headroom since increasing later remaps keys. Avoid excessive counts per broker because of memory, file handles and failover time.

Decides where a consumer starts when its group has no committed offset (or the offset was deleted by retention): earliest reads from the beginning, latest reads only new records, none throws an exception.

Sequential I/O on append-only segments, reliance on the OS page cache, zero-copy transfer from disk to network, batching and compression end to end, partition-level parallelism, and a simple pull model where brokers only track offsets.

qa.q: How would you replay messages from yesterday?
qa.a: Stop the consumer group, reset offsets with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-datetime, then restart (or use a new group id from earliest with a time filter). Consumers must be idempotent since records will be processed again.

qa.q: What happens if a producer sends to a partition whose leader is down?
qa.a: The send fails with a retriable error (NotLeaderOrFollowerException). The producer refreshes metadata, finds the newly elected leader (a follower from the ISR) and retries within delivery.timeout.ms. With acks=all and idempotence, no acknowledged data is lost or duplicated.

cheat.kafka-cheatsheet:
Architecture: brokers, topics, partitions, offsets

  • Kafka is a partitioned, replicated commit log; consumers pull by offset and data stays until retention.
  • Partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordering; consumer groups split partitions among members.
  • Leaders serve reads and writes; ISR followers replicate; KRaft replaced ZooKeeper.
  • Speed comes from sequential I/O, the page cache, zero-copy and batching.

Replication, ISR, high watermark and failover

  • Each partition has one leader; followers fetch from it, and the ISR is the set that has caught up.
  • Consumers read only up to the high watermark, so they never see records a failover could lose.
  • acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 on RF=3 survives one broker failure without losing acknowledged writes.
  • Leader epochs let a returning ex-leader truncate divergent records; keep unclean leader election off for critical data.

Partitioning, keys and ordering guarantees

  • Order is guaranteed only within a partition; use the entity id as the key.
  • Changing the partition count remaps keys and breaks per-key ordering across the change.
  • Hot keys overload one partition.
  • Idempotence keeps retries from reordering records.

Producer internals and configuration

  • send() batches per partition; a Sender thread ships batches to leaders.
  • Durable settings: acks=all, idempotence on, min.insync.replicas=2 with RF 3, no unclean leader election.
  • Throughput: linger.ms, batch.size, compression.type=zstd/lz4.
  • Keep send callbacks fast; they run on the I/O thread.

Consumer groups, offsets and rebalancing

  • Commit after processing for at-least-once; make processing idempotent.
  • max.poll.interval.ms exceeded → the consumer leaves the group → rebalance and duplicates.
  • Use cooperative sticky assignment and static membership to reduce rebalances.
  • More consumers than partitions sit idle.

Delivery semantics, idempotence and transactions

  • Idempotent producers dedup retries per partition using producer ids and sequence numbers.
  • Transactions commit output records and consumer offsets atomically; readers use read_committed.
  • Kafka EOS covers Kafka-to-Kafka only; external side effects still need idempotency or the outbox.
  • A stable transactional.id fences zombie producers.

Spring Kafka: producers, listeners, retries and DLT

  • Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer so poison pills don't loop forever.
  • DefaultErrorHandler with exponential backoff and DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer sends failures to a DLT.
  • @RetryableTopic gives non-blocking retries at the cost of per-key ordering.
  • Batch listeners enable bulk DB writes.

Retention, log compaction and schemas

  • Delete policy removes old segments by time or size; slow consumers past retention lose data.
  • Compaction keeps the latest value per key; null values are tombstones.
  • Use Avro/Protobuf with a Schema Registry and compatibility rules.
  • Events carry an id, type, timestamp, schema version and aggregate key.

Kafka Connect, CDC with Debezium and Kafka Streams

  • Kafka Connect moves data in and out of Kafka with configured source and sink connectors, no custom code.
  • Debezium CDC streams row changes from the database log and is the most robust outbox relay.
  • Kafka Streams is a library for stateful processing inside your service, backed by RocksDB and changelog topics.
  • A table is the latest value per key of a stream; KStream–KTable joins enrich events without remote calls.

Tuning, monitoring and troubleshooting

  • Consumer lag is the key metric; alert on its growth.
  • Fix lag by scaling consumers (up to partitions), speeding processing, or adding partitions.
  • Watch under-replicated partitions, offline partitions and ISR shrinks on brokers.
  • Kafka is a replayable log; RabbitMQ is a routing broker that deletes on ack.
